opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it gets at something a lot of people skip over.

When people talk about "AI improving AI," the picture is often an AI system that reads papers, runs experiments, tweaks architectures, and gradually makes itself better. I think that's a plausible direction. But if you look at how AI research is actually done today, a huge fraction of it is trial and error. We try a new optimizer, a new normalization, a new data mixture. Some things work, most don't, and often we don't really know why. It's closer to alchemy than to engineering.

If we hand that process to an AI, it may just do alchemy faster. It can search a larger space, but it's still blind search. The cost grows quickly, and the insights don't accumulate in a reusable form. You get a better model, but not a better understanding, and the next round of improvement starts almost from scratch.

That's where Physics of AI comes in. In physics, we don't just collect observations. We look for regularities, phenomena that show up again and again, and then build simple models that explain them. Scaling laws are an early example. Grokking, representation collapse, the edge of stability in optimization: these are phenomena we can study, model, and eventually predict. Once you have that kind of understanding, you're not searching blindly anymore. You can say, "Given this mechanism, this change should help, and here's roughly by how much."

So I see Physics of AI as building the "theory layer" that makes AI research compressible. It turns scattered empirical tricks into principles. And principles are exactly what an AI scientist needs to reason efficiently rather than brute-force. You can imagine an AI that knows the "physics" of training dynamics and representations proposing an improvement, predicting its effect, testing it, and updating the theory, the way a human physicist works, just much faster.

There's also a safety and trust side. If AI is improving AI, we want to understand what's changing and why. Physics-style understanding gives us handles: quantities to measure, laws to check against. Without that, we're just watching a loss curve go down and hoping.

So for me it's not a detour. It's the step that makes the whole loop scientific rather than just computational. First we need to understand AI the way physicists understand nature. Then AI can use that understanding, and eventually extend it, to improve itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes trial and error and a lack of reusable insights, but does not identify a shortage of well-structured, high-quality AI data as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It mentions uncertainty about why research changes work and says we may watch a loss curve go down and hope, but does not state that the mapping from training a model to its resulting training curve is poorly understood.

r003.rationale: The response says Physics of AI turns empirical tricks into principles, but does not say it is needed to structure data for AI-for-AI research.

r004.rationale: It describes an AI scientist testing improvements and updating theory like a human physicist, but much faster, and says AI can eventually extend Physics of AI understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Because right now, when we say "AI improves AI," what we actually mean is a very blind loop. We scale up, we try architectures, we run a sweep, we look at the loss curve, and we keep whatever worked. That's closer to alchemy than to engineering. It works, but nobody can tell you why it worked, and more importantly, nobody can tell you in advance what the next thing to try should be.

Think about how any other mature technology got to the point where it could improve itself. Before you had aerospace engineering, you had aerodynamics. Before you had electrical engineering, you had Maxwell's equations. You needed a layer of understanding that told you which quantities matter, how they relate, and what the boundaries of the design space actually are. Once you have that layer, improvement stops being trial and error and becomes design. You can predict, you can optimize, you can rule things out on paper.

Physics of AI is my attempt at building that layer for neural networks. By "physics" I don't mean importing specific equations from physics. I mean the methodology: find the simplest system that still shows the phenomenon, isolate the variables, do controlled experiments, and look for laws that generalize. Why does grokking happen? Why do scaling laws have the exponents they have? What is the network actually representing internally, and can we read it out? These are the questions where, if we had answers, an AI system trying to improve itself would have something to reason with instead of just something to search over.

And there's a second reason, which is about trust. If we eventually hand the job of improving AI to AI, we're going to want to understand what it's doing. If the improvement process is a black box operating on another black box, we've lost the ability to check it. A real science of these systems gives us the vocabulary to audit that process, to say "this change made the model better because of this mechanism," not just "the number went up."

So I see it as the bridge. On one side you have the empirical, scale-driven progress we have now. On the other side you have the dream of a self-improving system that we can still understand and steer. Physics of AI is what has to be built in between, because without it, the loop can run, but it runs blind, and I don't think we should be comfortable with a blind loop at that level of capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI improvement as blind trial and error, but does not identify a shortage of well-structured, high-quality AI data as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says the reasons for successful experiments are unclear and mentions examining loss curves, but does not state that the mapping from training a model to its resulting training curve is poorly understood.

r003.rationale: It presents Physics of AI as a methodology for understanding neural networks, but does not say it is needed to structure data for AI-for-AI research.

r004.rationale: The response says AI could reason better if Physics of AI supplied answers; it does not propose using AI to accelerate Physics of AI research.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between making AI better through trial and error and understanding why a particular change makes it better. We already use AI to help write code, design experiments, or search for better models. But if we don’t understand the underlying principles, we’re still doing a search—just a faster search.

By Physics of AI, I mean looking for simple principles that explain how learning works. What determines whether a model generalizes? How do useful representations emerge? Which aspects of a system actually control its behavior? The idea is to study simplified settings where we can isolate mechanisms, then see whether those mechanisms explain what happens in larger systems.

That gives AI something more useful than a collection of successful recipes. It gives it a framework for making predictions: if I change this part of the architecture or this part of the training process, what should happen, and why? Then it can propose experiments, test those predictions, and refine the theory.

So I wouldn’t say we need a complete physics of intelligence before AI can improve AI. That’s already happening in limited ways. But to make that improvement systematic and reliable, I think we need this intermediate step: turning empirical observations into understanding, and then using that understanding to guide the next improvement.

r002.rationale: It asks what determines generalization and how changes affect outcomes, but does not state that the mapping from training a model to its resulting training curve is poorly understood.

r003.rationale: Physics of AI is described as providing principles and a framework for predictions, not as a way to structure data for AI-for-AI research.

r004.rationale: The response says AI can propose experiments, test predictions, and refine theory, describing AI as a means to accelerate Physics of AI research.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if we want to use AI to improve AI, we need a way to tell whether we’re actually making progress. Today, a lot of AI research is empirical: we try something, train a model, and see whether the benchmark improves. An AI can help us do more of those experiments, but that alone doesn’t necessarily give us understanding.

What I mean by Physics of AI is finding simple principles behind these complicated systems. Can we identify the right quantities to measure, build a simplified model, and make predictions that experiments can test? We don’t need to understand every parameter. We need explanations that capture the mechanisms that matter.

That provides an intermediate step because it turns improving AI into a more structured scientific problem. AI can propose a hypothesis, design an experiment, compare the result with a prediction, and revise its explanation. Then it’s accumulating knowledge that can guide the next improvement, instead of just searching through more possibilities. The hope is that understanding makes that process much more efficient and reliable.
